To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there is evidence of a long run causal linkage running from stock market development to economic growth, (2) stock market development is an endogenous variable that is influenced by financial development and economic policy, (3) there is no evidence of a short run causal linkage running in either direction between stock market development and economic growth.
stock markets do have a positive effect on economic growth.
stock market development has a significant positive effect on economic growth in the short run and in the long run.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: Does a well functioning stock market promote economic development by stimulating the engine of growth, or does it promote it by better tuning it?
the relationship between financial development and economic performance.
the question whether a well developed stock exchange is a prerequisite for economic growth, and if it is, how this relationship works.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stock market is an integral part of the financial system and that the development of the stock market is likely to promote economic development in a country.
a stock market can foster growth in the long-run.
a well developed financial market is a key element in the process of economic development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stock market development can be considered as a key determinant of economic growth, but the relationship is not necessarily a simple one.
a well developed capital market can promote economic development.
the stock market development has a positive and significant impact on economic growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the causal relationship between stock market development and economic growth is not unidirectional, as it has been suggested by the literature so far.
the stock market can be a catalyst of economic growth, and that the stock market should therefore be a key component of the policy agenda.
causality inferences should not be based on bivariate causality analysis, as this may lead to invalid inferences.
